# **Software-Defined Radio Transmission via GPU Display Pipelines: Architectural Analysis and Benchmarking of Shader-Synthesized SSB and SSTV Emissions**

## **1\. State of the Art & Prior Art Benchmarking**

The repurposing of standard computing hardware for radio frequency synthesis occupies a unique junction between unintended electromagnetic compromising emanations (TEMPEST) and non-conventional software-defined radio (SDR) design. By manipulating raster graphics subsystems, high-speed digital buses, or peripheral clock trees, digital computing platforms can be transformed into functional RF transmitters without dedicated radio transmission silicon1.

### **Direct DAC and Video Output Synthesis**

The modern discipline of controlled electromagnetic emissions traces directly to the work of Markus Kuhn and Ross Anderson in their 1998 seminal paper on "Soft TEMPEST"4. Kuhn and Anderson demonstrated that the high-frequency electromagnetic emanations generated by cathode-ray tube (CRT) deflection coils and video cabling could be systematically shaped using targeted bitmap patterns5. By organizing pixels into alternating spatial patterns, the host computer synthesized controlled amplitude-modulated carriers and frequency-shift keyed (FSK) signals, enabling hidden data transmission across physical air gaps5.  
Erik Thiele operationalized this phenomenon in 2001 with the release of the open-source program *Tempest for Eliza*3. Thiele mapped audio melodies onto standard PC video display adapters by rendering alternating pixel patterns that radiated amplitude-modulated (AM) RF carriers in the medium-wave broadcast band, which were directly receivable on conventional AM radio receivers3. The underlying mechanism relied on the CPU computing pixel lines where spatial periodicities corresponded to the target RF carrier and the pixel intensity or pattern duty cycle corresponded to the audio modulation envelope10.  
In 2005, Fabrice Bellard demonstrated the direct synthesis of digital television (DVB-T) and analog television signals using a standard PC VGA card3. Bellard computed baseband representations of 2K-carrier Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) signals on the CPU, mapped the resulting values into the video framebuffer, and drove the video card's RAMDAC at high pixel clock rates3. By exploiting the higher-order harmonic images produced by the video DAC, Bellard radiated decodable broadcast television waveforms directly from the pins of a VGA connector into the VHF and UHF television bands3. While demonstrating the capability of video DACs to synthesize multi-megahertz complex digital modulations, Bellard's implementation relied entirely on CPU pre-calculation and repetitive static framebuffer buffers11.  
In 2009, Bartek Kania introduced *VGASIG*, an application that implemented real-time wideband frequency modulation (WBFM) broadcast transmission over the 88–108 MHz VHF FM band using a standard VGA graphics card3. Kania used the Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) to modify scanline pixel sequences on the CPU in real time, converting incoming audio samples into instantaneous frequency deviations3. A hardware-augmented approach was presented in 2013 by researcher "siro" at the hackerspace *das Labor*, who connected an external analog quadrature I/Q mixer to the Red and Green DAC output pins of a VGA adapter, driving the mixer with baseband analog quadrature signals generated by the video card3.  
In 2018, Steve Markgraf developed osmo-fl2k, which repurposed low-cost USB 3.0-to-VGA adapters based on the Fresco Logic FL2000 controller into transmit-only SDRs capable of operating at DAC rates up to 150 MSPS3. The FL2000 hardware architecture differs from conventional graphics adapters because it implements a software-defined display controller that streams raw byte samples directly from host memory across USB 3.0 Isochronous/Bulk transfers3. Markgraf disabled the hardware horizontal and vertical synchronization framing completely, transforming the adapter into an unconstrained, continuous 8-bit triple-DAC streaming transmitter capable of generating WBFM, GSM, GPS L1, and DVB-T signals3.  
In 2021, Paz Hameiri delivered a presentation at DEF CON 29 titled *TEMPEST Radio Station*, showing how GPU-accelerated workloads could intentionally radiate electromagnetic side channels9. Hameiri modulated electromagnetic leakage by controlling high-volume GPU memory copy transactions and clock line transitions, achieving covert digital audio streaming at 33 kbps over distances exceeding 50 feet9. More recently, Sun et al. published *TEMPEST-LoRa* at ACM CCS 2025, detailing a cross-technology covert communication channel that manipulates video streams across standard VGA and HDMI cabling1. By structuring pixel intensity sweeps, the authors produced standards-compliant Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS) packets receivable by off-the-shelf commercial LoRa gateways at ranges up to 87.5 meters1.

### **GPU-Accelerated RF Emission Paradigms**

Historically, video-based radio synthesis has been CPU-bound, with host software generating full raster buffers and copying them to video memory across the system PCIe bus1. While modern SDR frameworks utilize GPU compute pipelines (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan Compute) for reception tasks such as polyphase channelization, digital down-conversion (DDC), and high-resolution FFT analysis, the execution of transmit-side modulation algorithms directly inside GPU graphics rendering pipelines remains largely unexploited18.  
Executing direct digital synthesis (DDS) and quadrature up-conversion per-fragment inside fragment shaders (GLSL or HLSL) alters the throughput model of display-based SDR. Instead of transferring multimillion-sample arrays across the system bus for every frame, the host system uploads only low-bandwidth analytical baseband information into GPU texture memory19. The GPU's massive parallel shader core array evaluates the DDS carrier accumulator and mixer equations across billions of pixels per second at native display resolution and refresh rates, synthesizing high-frequency RF waveforms directly at the display interface20.

### **Comparison with Alternative Peripheral-Based SDR Hacks**

Display DAC radio synthesis differs fundamentally from other peripheral-based RF generation methods across the physical and spectral domains:

| Architecture / Method | Physical Transmission Mechanism | Output Waveform Characteristics | Typical Bandwidth & Data Rate | Spectral Purity & Harmonic Spurious Content |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **rpitx (Broadcom SoC)** \[cite: 3\] | Fractional PLL dividers driving GPCLK/PWM GPIO pins3. | 1-bit digital hard square wave3. | Fractional phase modulation; up to hundreds of kHz bandwidth. | Intense odd harmonic comb (![][image1]); requires multi-stage external filtering3. |
| **Ethernet PHY (LANtenna)** \[cite: 22, 23\] | Parasitic EMI from Cat5/6 twisted-pair cable line drivers22. | High-frequency burst noise induced by physical layer transitions22. | Extremely low; tens of bits per second22. | Non-linear line noise; wide spectral spread; no true phase or amplitude modulation control22. |
| **RAM Bus (GSMem, RAMBO)** \[cite: 24, 25\] | Electromagnetic leakage from multi-channel DDR3/4/5 memory buses24. | Clock harmonics modulated by memory read/write cycles25. | Low; 1 to 1000 bps symbol rates24. | Wideband switching noise; high phase jitter driven by operating system scheduling24. |
| **Display RAMDAC (Target PoC)** \[cite: 20, 21\] | Continuous analog voltage from 8-bit DAC driving 75 ![][image2] physical pin3. | Multi-level (256-step), continuous-time analog waveform3. | Full Nyquist bandwidth (![][image3]); supports high-fidelity audio/image modes. | Governed by sinc roll-off and periodic line blanking spurs; low close-in phase noise20. |

Compared to clock-divider hacks such as rpitx, which generate a 1-bit binary square wave with wideband odd harmonics, a video display RAMDAC is a true 8-bit multi-level digital-to-analog converter3. It synthesizes true multi-level amplitude and phase modulations with low intrinsic quantization noise3. Compared to bus-level covert channels (such as GSMem, AIR-FI, or SATAn), which rely on modulating the statistical power consumption of processor cores and memory controllers, display DAC synthesis is strictly deterministic22. The sampling rate is locked to a dedicated crystal oscillator driving the display timing controller, eliminating execution-dependent jitter and permitting phase-coherent communications1.

### **Complex Modulations on Raw Video DACs**

Prior research on video-based RF synthesis has remained confined to basic modulation formats:

> * Kuhn and Anderson (1998) utilized spatial square waves to generate continuous wave (CW) tones and binary frequency-shift keying6.  
> * Erik Thiele (2001) implemented double-sideband amplitude modulation (DSB-AM) for audio melodies3.  
> * Bartek Kania (2009) and Mordechai Guri (2014) synthesized analog wideband and narrowband FM by modulating carrier periods line-by-line2.  
> * Fabrice Bellard (2005) demonstrated digital OFDM transmission, but did so via static, pre-buffered baseband frames calculated offline on the CPU3.  
> * Sun et al. (2025) achieved Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation using pre-computed piecewise mathematical sweeps1.

Generating true single-sideband suppressed-carrier (SSB-SC) modulation or phase-continuous amateur Slow Scan Television (SSTV) directly on a standard video display controller has not been achieved in prior literature. Single-sideband modulation requires real-time analytical quadrature mixing (![][image4]) to suppress the unwanted sideband, a process that historically overwhelmed CPU frame allocators27. Furthermore, standard video raster graphics hardware imposes periodic blanking intervals between lines and frames, introducing phase discontinuities that corrupt continuous-phase modulation formats unless compensated for mathematically2.

## **2\. Novelty Evaluation of the Target Implementation**

The target proof-of-concept (PoC) introduces a hybrid host-GPU SDR transmission architecture. It synthesizes complex, bandwidth-efficient amateur radio modulations by utilizing standard desktop graphics hardware configured for 1080p@60Hz video output20.

### **End-to-End Signal Processing Architecture**

The architecture partitions computational responsibilities across the host CPU and the GPU graphics pipeline:  
The signal chain begins on the host CPU, which executes an amateur radio baseband engine generating Martin 1 Slow Scan Television (SSTV)27. The SSTV signal consists of a sequence of analog frequency-modulated audio tones occupying an audio bandwidth from 1200 Hz to 2300 Hz28. Specifically, horizontal synchronization pulses are encoded at 1200 Hz for 4.86 ms, followed by a 1500 Hz sync porch lasting 0.57 ms, and sequential color scan intervals for the Green, Blue, and Red channels lasting 57.15 ms each, separated by 1500 Hz separator pulses28.

### **Blanking Interval Compensation and Phase Continuity**

A fundamental obstacle in previous video-based SDR efforts was the disruption caused by video blanking intervals2. In standard video controllers, the DAC output is suppressed to the blanking level (![][image32]) during horizontal blanking (![][image36]) and vertical blanking (![][image37])3. If a DDS phase accumulator resets at the start of each line or frame, the carrier phase undergoes severe discontinuities, causing out-of-band splatter and corrupting phase-sensitive demodulators3.  
The evaluated architecture preserves carrier phase continuity mathematically across blanking intervals through host-GPU phase synchronization:

> * Host-side double-precision phase integration: The CPU maintains an un-aliased master phase accumulator in 64-bit floating-point precision (float64). Because the total number of pixel clock cycles in one complete video frame is constant (![][image38] clocks), the carrier phase advances over each frame by:

![][image39]

> * Hardware VSync locking: The application locks frame presentation to the display hardware vertical refresh rate using swap\_interval(1). Immediately prior to issuing the draw call for frame ![][image40], the host evaluates ![][image41] and transmits this value to the fragment shader as a uniform parameter.  
> * Virtual-raster intra-frame continuity: Within the shader, the sample index expression ![][image42] advances the phase as if the unrendered blanking pixels had been drawn sequentially. While the DAC output is physically gated off during blanking porches, the RF waveform resumes on the subsequent active scanline with the exact mathematical phase it would have possessed in an uninterrupted transmission, preventing line-rate and frame-rate phase slips2.

The target implementation achieves an **Originality Score of 9.4 / 10**.

| **Modulation Sophistication** | DSB-AM, CW tones, A-FSK, WBFM, piecewise CSS chirps1. | Analytic SSB-SC (![][image4] Hilbert pair) and phase-continuous Martin 1 SSTV27. | **Pioneering (9.8/10)**: First known realization of real-time single-sideband suppressed-carrier modulation on display hardware. |

| **Physical RF Interfacing** | Parasitic cable leakage or broad USB DAC streaming1. | Direct tap from VGA Pin 1 (Red RAMDAC) with 75-to-50 ![][image2] impedance matching20. | **Robust (9.1/10)**: Maximizes conducted signal-to-noise ratio compared to unintentional radiating loops. |

Previous work established that video hardware could generate electromagnetic signals, but implementations were constrained by architectural limitations3. Erik Thiele's *Tempest for Eliza* demonstrated AM synthesis on CRT monitors, but lacked phase synchronization and was limited to simple audio tones3. Bartek Kania's *VGASIG* demonstrated real-time FM, but relied on CPU-bound pixel generation that suffered from line-blanking phase ruptures3. Steve Markgraf's osmo-fl2k bypassed blanking entirely, but required a specific USB 3.0 chip operating in non-standard modes rather than functioning over standard GPU display pipelines3. The ACM CCS 2025 *TEMPEST-LoRa* research synthesized Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation via video cables, but operated via pre-calculated image patterns with low data throughput (21.6 bps)1.  
The target proof-of-concept establishes technical novelty by synthesizing complex, bandwidth-efficient amateur single-sideband modulation via GPU fragment shaders, executing real-time Hilbert-transformed analytical quadrature mixing at 148.5 MSPS while maintaining phase continuity across video blanking intervals20.

In addition to the zero-order hold sinc envelope, the physical analog output stage of the RAMDAC exhibits a continuous low-pass filter response governed by output pole capacitances and trace inductances3. Discrete and integrated triple 8-bit RAMDACs (such as the Analog Devices ADV7125 or internal GPU display PHYs) provide full-power analog bandwidths rated between 200 MHz and 330 MHz21. While operations within the fundamental Nyquist zone (such as 14.23 MHz on 20m or 50.1 MHz on 6m) incur minimal analog attenuation, attempts to exploit second-Nyquist-zone images (such as generating 144.20 MHz on 2m using a 4.3 MHz fundamental alias) suffer over 30 dB of sinc roll-off attenuation in addition to board-level trace filtering20.

| **GPU Shader SDR** *(Target PoC)* \[cite: 20, 21\] | Current | GPU Display RAMDAC (VGA Pin 1\)20 | Analytic SSB-SC & Martin 1 SSTV27 | HF Amateur Bands (e.g., 14.23 MHz)20 | Fragment shader 32-bit DDS & quadrature mixer20. | Line blanking generates spurs at 67.5 kHz needing filtering20. |

### **Originality Evaluation and Gap Analysis**

The evaluated proof-of-concept establishes architectural novelty across three technical domains:  
In contrast to previous video-based RF efforts, which required the CPU to calculate full-frame pixel buffers and stream them to video memory across the system bus, the target architecture migrates carrier direct digital synthesis and quadrature mixing into GPU fragment shaders1. The host CPU generates only an audio-rate (48 kHz) analytic baseband, which is uploaded to GPU memory as a texture19. The GPU fragment shader executes the 32-bit DDS phase accumulator and quadrature up-conversion per-pixel across the active raster area, generating an analog RF stream at the native 148.5 MSPS DAC rate without saturating host memory buses20.  
The target implementation achieves true single-sideband suppressed-carrier (SSB-SC) modulation directly on video hardware27. Prior works were restricted to double-sideband AM, CW tones, FM, or chirp-swept FSK1. By calculating the continuous analytic product:  
![][image30]  
the fragment shader suppresses the carrier and unwanted sideband in the mathematical domain prior to conversion by the RAMDAC, conserving spectral bandwidth and matching amateur radio voice and image transmission standards27.  
The architecture maintains continuous carrier phase tracking across video blanking intervals without requiring custom display controller modifications3. Previous display-based transmitters suffered severe phase ruptures across horizontal and vertical blanking intervals, causing spectral splatter and corrupting phase-sensitive demodulators2. By tracking total virtual pixels across line porches (![][image18]) and vertical blanking (![][image19]) in double-precision floating point on the host, and passing phase updates synchronized to vertical refresh via swap\_interval(1), the system maintains carrier phase alignment across frame boundaries20.  
The remaining technical constraint is the physical blanking pedestal: because the RAMDAC voltage is gated to ![][image32] during horizontal sync intervals, the output spectrum contains discrete sideband spurs spaced at multiples of ![][image162] at ![][image91]2. To achieve compliance with amateur radio emission standards (![][image114]), the physical output must be coupled through an impedance-matched low-pass filter to eliminate Nyquist images, accompanied by a sharp quartz crystal ladder filter to attenuate the close-in line rate spurs20.
